title: Gender Affirming Mastectomy Analgesia Rial
official: Paravertebral Versus Wide Local Infiltration for Analgesia Following Gender Affirming Mastectomy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
summary:
Introduction:

Optimizing pain management after gender-affirming mastectomy (removal of breast tissue, aka top surgery) surgery is important for recovery and minimizing opioid use. While paravertebral nerve blocks (numbing the chest wall through injections near the spine) and injection of local anesthetic ("skin freezing") are two commonly used methods, it's not clear which of these techniques is best among patients seeking gender-affirming care. Previous studies on nerve blocks in breast surgery have mostly concentrated on patients having breast cancer removed. Studies show that paravertebral blocks are superior to skin freezing in breast cancer surgery. However, it has not been established whether this reduces long-term pain and works similarly in gender-affirming top surgery. This study aims to compare the how well nerve blocks work comparing to skin freezing for pain and opioid use after surgery.

Research question:

Does the use of paravertebral nerve blocks, as compared to skin freezing (aka wide local infiltration), reduce need for opioid use within the first 24 hours following gender-affirming mastectomy?

Hypothesis:

The investigators hypothesize that paravertebral nerve blocks are superior to wide local infiltration in terms of reduced need for opioid consumption in the first 24 postoperative hours for gender-affirming mastectomy (GAM) patients.

Methodology:

This randomized control trial will include adult patients undergoing GAM. The patients will be randomly placed into the either the nerve block group or the skin freezing group. Patients who are in the skin freezing group will also be sent to the block room where they will receive ultrasound and pressure to mimic the feeling of receiving a block. Pain will be measured using the 0-10 Numeric Rating Scale, and opioid use will be recorded at 24-, 48-, and 72-hours post-op. Given that most patient leave hospital on the same day, participants will complete a pain journal at home and will be emailed an electronic survey to submit their results. Quality of recovery will be measured at 3 days after surgery. A follow-up survey at 3 months will assess longer term pain using the Brief Pain Inventory. Phone calls to complete the survey with a member of the research team can be done by request.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Adult (aged \>18 years) patients
* Undergoing gender affirming bilateral mastectomy
* Self-identifying with gender dysphoria

Exclusion Criteria:

* Severe pre-existing liver disease (Child B or C)
* Severe kidney disease (Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) \<30 (mL/min/1·73m²))
* Severe lung disease (modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale \> 2)
* An allergy to ropivacaine
* Weight \<50 kg
* Unable to provide valid consent to study prior to surgery
* BMI\>45

Justification for exclusion criteria Patients being excluded for liver disease, kidney disease, and low weight decreases the risk of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Known allergy to ropivacaine (the local anesthetic used in both groups) is to avoid anaphylaxis or other serious allergic reaction. Both types of blocks have a low risk of pneumothorax (injury to the lung); hence excluding patients with severe lung disease. Higher BMI (due to excess adipose tissue) increases the difficulty of nerve blocks, which could both increase risks and decrease success rates. Inability to provide consent interferes with the consent process. While a caregiver could provide consent on behalf the patient, the patient would not be able to complete self-rated scores, which are the central outcomes of this study.
